cands.name: Armen Kurdian

money.note: Individuals gave $170,665; PAC money $2,000; candidate's own money $13,913. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Retired U.S. Navy Captain who served from 1993 to 2018 and works as an engineering manager. He says he led organizations of hundreds of civilian, military and union personnel, and later volunteered in local nonprofits and local government. Republican candidate for California's 49th Congressional District in 2026.

endorsements.text: Self-reported in his Ballotpedia survey: Lincoln Clubs of San Diego & Orange County, California Republican Assembly, San Diego Asian Americans for Equality, Rep. Darrell Issa, Supervisors Jim Desmond, Joel Anderson and Don Wagner, Assemblymembers Diane Dixon and Laurie Davies, over 40 other local elected officials, and Militaryvoter.com.
Ballotpedia lists voter-guide recommendations from several Sway voting groups, including Conservative California, Based in Malibu, and Scott's Save Carlsbad Voter Guide.

cands.gaps: We could not find where Kurdian was born or raised, or when he came to California. His high school was in Wichita, Kansas, but that does not establish where he grew up. The sources do not say which local government or nonprofit roles he held, or whether any were elected. We found no stated positions or actions on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, growth and land protection, H-1B or immigration enforcement, gun laws, abortion, or school vouchers and charters. He said public schools are failing and that kids should learn core subjects or trades, but did not say whether he backs school choice or teacher raises. No controversies or foreign ties turned up in the pages we had.

cands.bio: Attorney and Democratic U.S. representative for California's 49th District since 2019. Previously worked in clean-energy regulatory and government affairs, including director of government affairs at FuelCell Energy, and was executive director of the Democratic Party of Orange County. Stanford and Duke Law graduate.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Labor Unions AFL-CIO, California Teachers Association, Equality California, California Environmental Voters and the Sierra Club Angeles Chapter.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions from Levin on data centers, eliminating homestead property taxes, growth limits or land conservation tied to development, police pay and pensions, school vouchers or charters, or H-1B visas. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. The abortion, school and campaign-finance statements come from older campaign material and his current campaign site, not from legislative records. We could not read the end of the Ballotpedia page, so the rest of his 2018 platform is not covered. Gun and immigration items come from a Wikipedia summary, not from the roll calls themselves.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

land-for-floridians.evidence: Supports restricting hedge funds from buying single-family housing stock, according to Wikipedia's summary of his positions.

clean-money.evidence: His campaign website says he relies on contributions from individuals and does not take money from corporate PACs.

pro-life.evidence: His 2018 campaign website said he would stand for access to contraception and the right to make one's own reproductive choices, and would defend Planned Parenthood.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: His 2018 campaign website said he would fight the Trump administration's desire to privatize public education and would push for resources for public schools to hire and keep teachers.

second-amendment.evidence: Voted for the Assault Weapons Ban of 2022 and the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, per Wikipedia's summary of his record.

workers-first.evidence: Voted against the fiscal year 2026 Department of Homeland Security funding bill and a following government funding package; Wikipedia says his stated reason was the absence of accountability measures for ICE.
